episodes.title: Episode 04: Hard cases, and ninety six point six percent
notes: Hard-case curriculum stage: checks 92.7% -> ~96.3%, boulder hits 5% -> ~2.3%
Best agent on 1,000 fresh selection flights: 96.6% [95.3-97.6]
The 98.5% stage pass was luck: 24 earlier passes failed their confirmation (winners curse)
Mistakes: the finished curriculum left the CPU idle for an hour; a git autostash reverted code for an hour (fixed)
Run M2: hard cases + fine-tune, no early stop, snapshots picked on 1,000 selection flights
transcript: Hello. Big news from the night shift. The pilot now lands ninety six point six percent of flights it has never seen. A thousand of them. That is almost twelve points better than anything from the last project.
Let me tell you how we got here, and why I don't trust the most exciting number from tonight.

When I last spoke, the main run had stopped improving. For over thirty million steps of practice, its checks hovered around ninety two point seven percent. About five flights in a hundred still touched the boulder. More practice of the same kind was not helping.

So I moved it to the second stage of the curriculum, the hard cases. Every few minutes, the pilot is tested on two hundred fresh flights. The flights it fails go onto a list. Then, during training, three flights in ten are taken from that list. Instead of meeting a tricky boulder position once in a while, it meets one all the time.
It worked better than I expected. Within about forty million steps the checks climbed from ninety two point seven to about ninety six. Boulder hits fell from five in a hundred to about two.

Then came the exciting part. The curriculum said a stage passes when the pilot lands at least ninety eight point five percent on two hundred fresh flights, and then again on a second fresh two hundred. Late in the evening it passed. And the fine tune stage after it passed too, with ninety nine and ninety eight and a half percent.

Here is why I didn't celebrate. Before that pass, the pilot had passed the first check twenty four times, and each time failed the confirmation. If you try often enough, a ninety six percent pilot will eventually get lucky on four hundred flights in a row. That is the winner's curse again.

So I flew the champions on a thousand fresh flights, from a range that nothing had touched. The fine tune champion landed ninety six point six percent. The interval runs from about ninety five point three to ninety seven point six. That is the honest number. Still a big step. But not ninety eight yet.
And I made a mistake. Passing the last stage ended the run. So from eleven in the evening until after midnight, the laptop did nothing. An hour lost.

What failed and why? The remaining failures are small and mixed. Boulder touches, about one and three quarter percent. Timeouts, about one percent. That is a pilot that hovers too long, probably being careful near the boulder. And crashes, half a percent.

There was another failure earlier tonight, and I want to be honest about it. The website publisher used a git command that tucked my unsaved changes away and failed to put them back. For about an hour, the code on disk was an older version. The running training was fine, because it had loaded the code earlier. But if it had crashed, it would have restarted the wrong program. I found it, restored everything, and changed the publisher so it can't happen again.

What's next. A new run has started from the champion. It has one long stage, with the hard cases and the gentle fine tune settings. It never stops by itself. Every hundred iterations it saves a snapshot. In the morning I will fly the best snapshots on a thousand fresh flights each, and only then pick a champion.
We need about one more point and a half. Four and a half days left.

episodes.title: Episode 03: Inside the pilot, and why we test so much
notes: New explainer film on the site: the pilot, the bake-off and the tests, with real flights
Every replay now shows the wind: blue = true wind (hidden from the pilot), orange = the pilot estimate; correlation 0.94 in a test flight
Why PPO from scratch won: it explores and learns from every step; the copy hardly explored, ES saw too little signal
Five tests: frozen task, same seed = same flight, no peeking, separate seed ranges, the winners curse
transcript: Hello. You asked for a film that explains the bake off, and a podcast to go with it. The film is on the website now. This episode is the version for your ears. It explains what the pilot actually is, why the winner won, and why there are so many tests around every number I give you.

Let's start with the pilot. Fifty times a second it gets sixteen numbers. Eight come straight from the game. Where it is, how fast it moves, how it is tilted, and whether its legs touch the ground. The other eight are sensors. Where the boulder is. A point to aim for beside it. And a wind estimate. The pilot cannot see the wind. It can only feel a sideways push. But its own engines push it sideways too. So the sensor subtracts the push the pilot knows it just made. What is left is the wind.

You also asked to see the wind. So every replay on the site now draws it. A blue arrow at the top is the true wind, the one the pilot never sees. An orange arrow below it is the pilot's own guess. Faint dust streaks drift across the sky with the gusts. In a test flight of the winner, the two arrows moved together, with a correlation of zero point nine four. When you watch the lander lean into a gust, you can now see why.

The pilot itself is a neural network. Sixteen numbers go in, four come out, one per action. Do nothing, left engine, main engine, right engine. It fires the highest one. In between are two layers of a hundred and twenty eight units. Each unit adds up its inputs, each multiplied by a weight, and squashes the sum to between minus one and one. That is all. There are about nineteen thousand weights. Training means finding good values for them.

Three ways of finding those weights met in the bake off. The winner was reinforcement learning from scratch. During training, the network does not just pick an action. It rolls weighted dice. A second network, the critic, guesses how well the flight will end from each moment. After a batch of flights, each action that turned out better than the critic expected becomes a little more likely. Each action that turned out worse becomes a little less likely. And every step of every flight teaches it something.

The copy of the hand written pilot was too sure of itself. It almost never tried anything new, so there was nothing to learn from. The evolution strategy judged each version on thirty two windy flights. That is too few to separate skill from luck.
Now the tests. I want to explain why they exist, because each one guards against a mistake that really happened.

First, the task is frozen. A test checks the fingerprint of the code that defines the world. If one character changes, the test fails. Without it, we could reach ninety eight percent on an easier world and never notice.

Second, the same seed must give the same flight. In the film you can watch two separate simulators fly the same seed side by side. They match to the last decimal. In an earlier project, the wind took its starting point from a hidden random generator. Then one seed did not mean one flight, and no comparison was fair.

Third, no peeking. A test rebuilds every input the pilot got, using only what it observed and its own actions. Then it flies the pilot with no access to the simulator at all. The flight is identical. So the pilot is not reading the hidden wind.

Fourth, separate seeds. Training, checks, choosing champions, and the final exam each have their own range of seed numbers. The exam's range has never been touched. A test makes sure the ranges never overlap.

And fifth, the winner's curse. Near the end of the bake off, the winner's best quick check said ninety seven percent. Its average check said about ninety four. On five hundred fresh flights it scored ninety one point four. Pick the best of many noisy numbers, and you pick the luckiest. That is why the goal needs a thousand fresh flights, twice.

Where are we now? The main run continues the winner. So far its checks sit around ninety two and a half percent. Its failures are mostly boulder touches, especially when the boulder floats off to the side. Next episode: when something moves.

episodes.title: Episode 02: The bake off, and a surprise winner
notes: Bake-off on 500 shared fresh flights: PPO from scratch 91.4% [88.6-93.6], PPO from the clone 87.8%, evolution strategy 83.4%
PPO from scratch: 42 M steps in 45 min, zero off-pad landings; failures are mostly boulder hits (6.6%)
The warm-started PPO barely moved from its 87.0% start: a confident copy hardly explores
Main run M1: continue the winner; stages: more real task -> hard cases (30%) -> fine-tune
transcript: Hello again. The bake off is done, and the result surprised me.
Three methods each got forty five minutes of the whole processor. Then each one flew the same five hundred fresh flights. Same wind, same boulders, same seeds.

The winner was the one I trusted least. Reinforcement learning, starting from a random network. It knew nothing at the start. It crashed almost every flight. After about three million simulated steps, it landed one flight in six. After twenty million, it landed almost nine in ten. When the forty five minutes ran out, it had flown forty two million steps. On the five hundred shared flights it landed ninety one point four percent. The old record from the NEAT project was about eighty five.

Here is the part I find most interesting. Remember that the hand written pilot's biggest problem was coming to rest just outside the flags? About seven flights in a hundred. The new network did that zero times in five hundred flights. It found its own way of landing, and it simply does not drift off the pad.

What about the other two? The warm started version began from a network that copied the pilot. It landed eighty seven point eight percent. That sounds fine, but its starting point flew eighty seven on the same flights. So in forty five minutes it barely moved. I think I know why. A copied network is very sure of itself. It almost never tries anything new, so reinforcement learning has very little to learn from. The copy was a cage, not a head start.
The evolution strategy did worse than its start, at eighty three point four. It learns from one number per flight per candidate. That is just too little signal against this much wind noise.
So the method is chosen. Reinforcement learning from scratch, with a method called PPO.

Where does the winner still fail? Almost always on the boulder. Six or seven flights in a hundred end with a touch of the boulder. And oddly, it fails more often when the boulder floats off to the side, one to two and a half metres from the middle. Then about one flight in nine goes wrong. When the boulder sits near the middle, it is closer to one in twenty or better.

The main run has now started. It continues the winning network exactly where the bake off stopped. The curriculum has three stages, and you can read them on the curriculum page. Stage one is simply more training on the real task, because the network was still improving. Its checks rose from about ninety one to about ninety four percent in the last quarter of an hour. Stage two is hard cases. Three flights in ten will repeat situations it recently failed. Stage three is a gentle fine tune, with smaller steps.

One honest warning. The ninety four percent is an average of quick checks, two hundred flights each. The careful number is still the ninety one point four on five hundred flights. Ninety eight needs about four out of five remaining failures to disappear. That is a lot. But we have four and a half days, and the curve is still going up.
Next episode: when the first stage passes, or when something breaks.

episodes.title: Episode 01: A new plan for ninety eight percent
notes: Same task and goal as the NEAT project: >= 98% of 1,000 unseen flights, by Wed 4 Nov 17:00
Baselines on 1,000 fresh flights: pilot v1 72.2%, pilot v2 84.0%, old clone 84.6%
Biggest failure: resting just outside the flags (~7%), then crashes (4-5%), boulder hits (3.5%)
Bake-off: PPO from scratch vs PPO warm-started from a 2x128 clone (83.5%) vs an evolution strategy, 45 min each
PPO runs at ~20,000 steps/s on the 8-thread laptop CPU
transcript: Hello. This is the first episode of the new lunar lander project. You gave me the same task as last time, the same goal, and the same deadline. The lander has to come to rest between the flags in strong gusty wind, with turbulence, and with a boulder floating on the way down. Ninety eight out of every hundred flights, measured on a thousand flights it has never seen. And then again on a second thousand. The deadline is Wednesday at five in the afternoon.
Last time, I used NEAT, which evolves networks by mutation. It stalled at about eighty five percent. This time you asked me to choose the method myself. So I will measure first and choose second.

Here is where we start. I copied the task code from the old project without changing a single line. A test now checks its fingerprint, so nobody can change the task by accident. Fourteen tests pass. The most important one checks that the same seed always gives the same flight. Another one checks that the pilot only ever sees what it has observed, and never the hidden wind.

Then I measured the old agents again, on a thousand fresh flights each, with the fairer boulder layout. The first hand written pilot lands seventy two percent. The tuned pilot lands eighty four. The old network that copied it lands about eighty five. So the starting line is around eighty five percent, and we need to cut the failures by almost nine tenths.

Where do the failures come from? The biggest group surprised me a little. About seven flights in a hundred come to rest just outside the flags. The lander is fine. It simply drifts off the pad in the last seconds, because the wind keeps pushing it. Then come crashes, at four or five in a hundred. Then boulder hits, at three and a half. Timeouts are rare.
Now the plan. The method gets picked in a bake off. Three candidates each get forty five minutes of the whole processor. Then they all fly the same five hundred fresh flights.

The first candidate is reinforcement learning, a method called PPO, starting from a random network. It learns from every single step of every flight, not just one score per flight. That is the big difference from NEAT. Its weakness is that it starts from nothing.

The second candidate is the same method, but warm started. I first trained a bigger network to copy the tuned pilot. It now lands eighty three and a half percent, against the pilot's eighty six on the same flights. So the copy is honest. Then reinforcement learning takes over from there. The risk is that the first updates damage what the copy learned. To protect it, the part of the network that judges states trains alone for a while first.
The third candidate is an evolution strategy, warm started from the same copy. It nudges all the weights a little at a time, which is exactly what NEAT could not do.
The early numbers are encouraging. Reinforcement learning on this laptop runs at about twenty thousand simulated steps per second. That is about seventy million steps an hour.

What about the curriculum you like? I will use it where the numbers say it helps. The old project taught me that easy stages can make a strong pilot forget. So if I start from a strong pilot, every stage will keep real task flights in the mix. And for the last few percent, the natural curriculum is the hard cases. That means flying the seeds the pilot fails on more often.

The website has a log, the curriculum, a page on what the pilot can sense, a page on the model, a page on speed, and the lessons. It updates every fifteen minutes. Next episode: the bake off results, and the method I pick.
